raw_case_text:
In this case, a 31-year-old female presented with progressive pain and decreased range of motion of her left hip over 2 months, and the pain had increased progressively and worsened with activity. During the 2 months, the patient reported fever and had self-administered cephalosporin antibiotics. She had no history of chills, fatigue, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. However, she mentioned her husband was being treated for "tuberculosis". Physical examination revealed pain in flexion, adduction, and external rotation of the left acetabulum, but no swelling, local skin damage, ecchymosis, or obvious local deformity. It showed no respiratory and neurologic symptoms or signs. Laboratory investigations showed a serum C-reactive protein level of 67.51 mg/L, total white blood cell count of 7700/mm3 with 86.8% neutrophils, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 64 mm/h. The viral serology tests for hepatitis B yielded positive results and suggested chronic hepatitis B. The HIV screening, Mycobacterium tuberculosis antibody, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA tests were all negative.
Radiographs demonstrated a 3 cm purely lytic lesion in the left acetabulum without sclerosis or periosteal reaction. The continuity of the local cortical bone was interrupted, and the adjacent soft tissues were inflamed (Fig. 1a). Computed tomography (CT) scan showed osteolytic bone destruction of the left acetabulum with clear borders and no sclerosed margins, and a soft tissue mass measuring 3.5 cm by 2.0 cm by 3.3 cm in the left acetabulum. The average CT value was approximately 44HU (Fig. 1b, c). The wall was strengthened with a CT value of 76HU, and there was a liquid low-density shadow in the mass with a CT value of 23HU, and no enhancement was seen (Fig. 1d, e). Three-dimensional reconstruction showed bone destruction in the left acetabulum (Fig. 1f). Chest CT showed bullae at the apical segment of the right upper lobe, with the remainder of the chest showing no obvious abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed irregular bone destruction and abscess formation in the left acetabulum, with the abscess measuring 3.6 cm by 1.9 cm by 3.5 cm, cortex erosion and significant bone and soft tissue edema were also observed (Fig. 2a-c). The presence of enhancement at the edge of the lesion and an area of liquefaction necrosis without enhancement in the center indicate abscess formation (Fig. 2d-f). Imaging diagnosis of infectious disease with abscess formation.
The mass was sampled by fine-needle aspiration biopsy under ultrasound guidance. Histopathological examination of the specimen showed granulomatous inflammation surrounded by a large number of multinuclear giant cells, some lymphocytes, and plasma cells (Fig. 3a, b), and the presence of Cryptococcus was confirmed by periodic acid-Schiff's reaction (Fig. 3c). The resulting histopathological diagnosis was granuloma with Cryptococcus.
After one month of antifungal treatment with fluconazole and flucytosine, a fungal culture from diseased tissue secretions produced a negative result. Upon discharge, the left leg was placed under traction and immobilized to prevent hip dislocation and relieve the pain, and we continued the antifungal treatment. A follow-up of MRI after 10 months confirmed a decrease in the lesion's size (from 3.6 cm by 1.9 cm by 3.5 cm to approximately 2.7 cm by 1.6 cm by 3.1 cm), but there was still some bone defect in the left acetabulum (Fig. 4).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old female presented with a 2-month history of progressive left hip pain and decreased range of motion accompanied by fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2 months prior to presentation, the patient experienced progressively worsening left hip pain that was aggravated by activity and associated with restricted range of motion and fever. She had self-administered cephalosporin antibiotics without relief.
subjective.past_medical_history: Husband was undergoing treatment for tuberculosis. Chronic hepatitis B identified on workup.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive left hip pain, limited range of motion, and fever. Negative for chills, fatigue, weight loss, respiratory symptoms, or neurological symptoms. Self-administered oral cephalosporins prior to admission.

objective.physical_examination: Left hip examination revealed pain on flexion, adduction, and external rotation of the left acetabulum, without local swelling, skin damage, ecchymosis, or obvious deformity. No respiratory or neurological signs were present.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum CRP 67.51 mg/L, WBC 7700/mm3 (86.8% neutrophils), ESR 64 mm/h. Hepatitis B viral serology was positive (consistent with chronic hepatitis B). HIV screening, Mycobacterium tuberculosis antibody, and M. tuberculosis DNA tests were negative. Hip radiographs showed a 3 cm purely lytic lesion in the left acetabulum with cortical interruption and adjacent soft tissue inflammation without sclerosis or periosteal reaction.
objective.advanced_workup: Pelvic CT and 3D reconstruction showed osteolytic destruction of the left acetabulum with clear borders and a 3.5 x 2.0 x 3.3 cm soft tissue mass (mean 44 HU, wall enhancement 76 HU, central liquid low-density 23 HU). Chest CT showed right upper lobe apical bullae with no other abnormalities. Hip MRI showed irregular bone destruction, cortex erosion, bone/soft tissue edema, and a rim-enhancing abscess measuring 3.6 x 1.9 x 3.5 cm in the left acetabulum. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass showed granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of primary isolated cryptococcal osteomyelitis and abscess of the left acetabulum, confirmed by ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy histopathology showing granulomatous inflammation and encapsulated yeast positive on periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining; tuberculosis and HIV were excluded. Treated with antifungal combination therapy using fluconazole and flucytosine, achieving negative fungal culture from tissue secretions after 1 month, along with left lower extremity traction and immobilization to prevent hip dislocation. At 10-month MRI follow-up, the acetabular lesion had decreased from 3.6 x 1.9 x 3.5 cm to 2.7 x 1.6 x 3.1 cm with residual bone defect.
